entries.meaning: Then the vulture spoke with composure: ‘Hear me, Rāma, destroyer of the fear of becoming. Lord, the ten-headed Rāvaṇa has brought me to this state; that villain abducted Janaka's daughter and carried her south while she lamented bitterly like an osprey. I kept my life only to see you, Lord; now, treasury of grace, I wish to depart.’ Rāma told his father-like friend to preserve his body, but Jaṭāyu smiled and replied: ‘The Vedas sing that even the lowest person is liberated if your Name comes to his lips at death. You stand visibly before my eyes—Lord, for what want should I retain this body?’ With tears filling his eyes, Rāma said, ‘Father, through your own deed you have gained the highest destiny. Nothing in the world is difficult for those whose hearts are devoted to another's welfare. Relinquish the body and go to my abode; what can I give you, who are desire fulfilled? Father, do not tell my father of Sītā's abduction when you reach him. If I am truly Rāma, the ten-headed one himself will come with his lineage and tell him.’
The vulture relinquished his body and assumed Hari's form, adorned with many ornaments, incomparable yellow garments, a dark body and four broad arms. With tears filling his eyes, he offered praise.

Rāma is supremely tender-hearted, compassionate to the helpless and gracious without cause. He granted to a lowly, flesh-eating bird the destiny that yogins seek. Hear, Umā: unfortunate are those who abandon Hari and become attached to sense objects. The two brothers resumed searching for Sītā, walking through the vast forest and looking everywhere. The dense wood was crowded with vines, trees, birds, deer, elephants and lions. On their path they struck down Kabandha, who recounted his curse: ‘Durvāsā cursed me; seeing the Lord's feet has erased that sin.’ Rāma said, ‘Hear, Gandharva, I tell you: one who hates the Brahmin lineage does not please me. But whoever abandons deceit in mind, deed and speech and serves the earth-gods, the Brahmins, brings me, Brahmā, Śiva and every god under his loving influence.’

The passage says that saints sing of a Brahmin as worthy of reverence even when cursing, striking or speaking harshly; it directs one to honour a Brahmin lacking conduct and virtue, but not a Śūdra even when rich in virtues and accomplished in knowledge. Having explained this inherited social dharma to Kabandha, Rāma was pleased to see his love for the Lord's own feet. Bowing his head to Rāma's lotus feet, Kabandha rose into the sky and attained his proper destiny. Having granted him liberation, generous Rāma stepped into Śabarī's hermitage. Seeing Rāma enter her home, Śabarī remembered her teacher's words and they delighted her heart. Lotus-eyed Rāma wore a crown of matted locks and a forest garland upon his broad chest; the two brothers, one dark and one fair, were beautiful. Śabarī fell and clung to their feet. Immersed in love, no speech came to her mouth; again and again she bowed her head to the lotus feet. Respectfully bringing water, she washed their feet, seated them on lovely seats, and brought supremely delicious tubers, roots and fruits for Rāma. The Lord ate them lovingly and praised them again and again.

Śabarī stood before Rāma with joined hands; beholding him, her love increased immensely. She said, ‘How can I praise you? I am of a lowly community and very dull-minded; among those deemed low, women are called lower still, and among them I am slow-minded and sinful.’ Rāma replied, ‘Hear me, noble lady: I recognize only the bond of devotion. Social group, rank, lineage, dharma, eminence, wealth, strength, family, virtues and cleverness—how can a person without devotion shine? He appears like a cloud without water. I shall tell you the ninefold devotion; listen attentively and hold it within your mind. The first devotion is company with saints; the second is love for accounts of my deeds; the third is humble service to the teacher's lotus feet; and the fourth is singing the multitude of my virtues after abandoning deceit.’

Rāma continued: ‘The fifth devotion, proclaimed by the Vedas, is mantra-recitation and worship of me with firm trust. The sixth is self-restraint, good conduct, detachment from excessive activity, and continual dedication to the dharma of good people. The seventh is seeing the world equally as filled with me and esteeming saints as greater than me. The eighth is contentment with whatever comes and never seeing another's fault, even in dream. The ninth is simplicity and freedom from deceit toward everyone, trust in me within the heart, and being neither elated nor dejected. Whoever possesses even one of these nine—woman, man, or any moving or unmoving being—is exceedingly dear to me, noble lady. Every form of devotion is firmly present in you. The destiny difficult for assemblies of yogins has today become easy for you. The supreme, incomparable fruit of seeing me is that the soul attains its own innate form. Noble lady, if you know news of Janaka's daughter, tell me, elephant-gaited one.’ Śabarī replied, ‘Go to Lake Pampā, Rāma; there you will form friendship with Sugrīva. He will tell everything, divine hero of Raghu—though you know, steadfast wise one, you ask me.’ Again and again she bowed her head at the Lord's feet and lovingly related the whole account.
